title: How I built my blog
body:
I got the urge to build a blog site after I saw Vasilios Syrakis’ site where he’s using Zola and Duckquill. For me I thought this was the perfect place where I could share my own work and other things. I always wanted a space where I could dish out my own thoughts and opinions without the need to perform a certain way or post certain topics.
To begin I researched how could I host such site without tearing my hair out. At first I tought the way to do it would be using a VPS. This wouldn’t be the way as I was looking at it more and more. Then I discovered that Cloudflare provides a service called ‘Cloudflare Pages’. Its essentialy a more automated way to create static sites.
Luckily I already had a domain registered at cloudflare, so I was sort of familiar with the dashboard. Using the zola docs, I followed the instructions on how to create a Zola site with Pages. The link to the guide is here.
That was the hosting part. Now came the actual building of the site. At first I was confused how Zola initialy worked. I expected it would be an engine running on a server, that would create sites using commands.
In reality it isn’t installed on a server, but on a client device. The user creates and edits the sites on their device. When they have edited everything they needed, they then use git to update the repository. When the repository is updated the Cloudflare Pages worker checks the repo for new updates. When new updates are detected, it starts creating/mirroring in the changes in repository. After it’s gone through the changes Pages then publishes the site.
So now we have talked about hosting and building, but we also need a theme for our site. Duckquill struck me as perfect theme for blog site. It’s relatively simple, however I do like the simple aesthetic of it. I understand it’s not everyones cup of tea, but it’s my site not yours.
This was the hardest part for me to figure out, since I never worked with markdown or anything of that sort.
The repo had already a few examples on how sites would look. I simply copy and pasted the examples to my blog and using trial and error method I slowly was shaping my idea for this blog site. It’s not perfect, it might not even be good. But I am happy with how it turned out.
I want to keep this blog short. I wanted to do a step by step guide on how to set this up, but I got lazy and just wanted to put my experience out there. You can set it up on your own without anyones help. I know I did. It’s not perfect, but I like the way it turned out.
Thank you to Vasilios Syrakis, daudix (creator of duckquill), Vincent Prouillet and other contributors of Zola for making these tools and inspirations.
If you have any questions or feedback please send me an email: stepan@bargl.org

title: German: Unit one
body:
Spelling:
All nouns in German are written with capital letters regardless of location in a sentence (Example: Der Mann und die Frau arbeiten jeden Tag am Computer)
pronoun ich (I) has no initial capital, but Sie (you) has
Different characters:
ß is called es·tset,
comes after ei, ie, or a, o, u
heißen - to be called
Straße - street
groß - big
umlauts ä, ö, ü
change the pronunciation of a word and its meaning
Mutter is mother, but Mütter is mothers
Mustte means had to, but Müstte means should
Three genders
Nouns are either masculine, feminine or neuter
articles: der for masculine, die for feminine, das for neuter
Grammatical not biological
der Tisch - the table (masculine)
die Tür - the door (feminine)
das Fenster - the window (neuter)
Best to learn a new noun is with articles
Endings
German words take specific endings depending on their relationship to other parts of the sentence.
This applies to verbs, articles and possessive adjectives and adjectives
Verbs
Describe the action of a sentence, such as “to run”, “to think”
German “to go” has different endings when used with “I”, “he” and “they”
Ich gehe - I go
Er geht - He goes
Sie gehen - They go
Articles and possessive adjectives
words are linked to a noun such as “a”, “the”, “my” or “his”
indefinite article “a” changes in German when it is linked to the subject of the sentence (ein Mann) or the object of the sentence (einen Mann)
Ist das ein Mann? - Is that a man?
Da drüben sehe ich einen Mann. - I can see a man there.
Adjectives
describe the quality of a noun
In German adjectives have different endings when they are linked to different genders
ein neuer Computer
eine intteligente Frau
ein schönes Haus
Cases
You can tell what function a noun performs based on its ending and the form of the article
A noun can be the subject of the sentence, the agent of what is happening
Der Hund beißt den Mann.
Or it can be the object, the receiver of the action
Der Hund beißt den Mann
The subject and the object are in different cases, which means that the article has a different ending.
Both “dog” and “man” are masculine (der) but “the dog” (der Hund) is the subject and “the man” (den Mann) is the object.
Word order
Word order is flexible in German
Position of the finite verb matters
The finite verb is the second idea in most statements:
Er hat zwei Brüder
Morgen fahre ich nach Manchester
Finite verbs goes the beginning of orders and questions:
Öffnet das Fenster!
Hast Du morge Zeit?
Finite verb goes at the end in subordinate clauses:
Ich kann morgen nicht kommen, weil ich nach Manchester fahre.
If there are two verb forms, one of them goes at the end
Morgen muss ich nach Manchster fahren.
Tenses
In English tenses differentiate between an action happening at the moment (‘I am working’) and an action taking place regularly (‘I work at Harrods’)
In German the finite verb form is the same in both statements
Ich arbeite
Ich arbeite bei Harrods
Past tense in english is expressed either by present perfect tense or simple past tense
German is simpler: normally use the present perfect when you talk about the past regardless of when it happend
The simple past is used in written German
Checklist
Where do you use capital letters in German? - All nouns are written with capital letters regardless of the location in the sentence.
When do you use the letter ß? - after ie, ei or a, o, u
Why are umlauts important? - They can change the form a noun Mütter is ‘mothers’ but Mutter is ‘mother’
What is the difference between the use of gender in German and English? - Nouns are either masculine, feminine or neuter. We use articles der for masculine nouns, die for feminine nouns and das for Neuter nouns
Give an example where a word changes its ending in German. - Ich gehe, Er geht
What is one of the most important principles affecting German word order? - The position of the finite verb.
Is there a difference between ‘I am working’ and ‘I work’ in German? No, there is no difference. Ich arbeite and Ich arbeite
Source: Basic German - A Grammar and Workbook by Heiner Schenke and Karen Seago
